observations: In the lower map a broad pink band runs from Kowno on the left, rising and narrowing across the sheet to Moscou at the upper right.
A thin black band returns from Moscou back toward the left edge, running beneath the pink band; a temperature graph sits along the bottom.
An upper map traces a second, narrower pink band from Spain across southern Gaul to the Alps.
effect: The continuous bands carry the eye along the route out and back, so the reader follows the campaign as a journey before reading the labels.
teaching_value: A nineteenth-century information graphic uses a single directional band as the reading path; its width also encodes quantity, so it teaches flow lines in charts and maps.
ambiguity: Band width (scale) carries the data as strongly as direction; this reading counts the path the eye follows, not the statistical encoding.

observations: A very large green circle with a pink inner circle sits at the far left, labelled Empire Russe.
To its right a row of progressively smaller circles sits on one baseline, ending in small circles labelled Prusse, France pays and Portugal.
Vertical lines rise from each circle against a ruled grid, joined by dotted diagonals.
effect: Placing one huge circle beside a row of much smaller ones makes the difference in extent readable at a glance before any figure is read.
teaching_value: An early statistical chart compares quantities by circle size on a common baseline; a clear historical model for size as data in information design.
ambiguity: Circle area versus diameter is not stated on the chart, so the exact proportional rule is not established from the pixels.

observations: Nineteen occupation names are listed down the left, each with a crimson horizontal bar; the top bar runs almost the full width.
From Railroad employees down to Hostlers the bars are short stubs, and a tall curly bracket gathers them.
The bracket points to a single longer crimson bar set off to the right of the stubs.
effect: Bracketing the many short bars and showing their total as one bar lets small categories be read as one group without losing the individual rows.
teaching_value: A hand-drawn 1900 data portrait groups a long tail of small values with a bracket and a combined bar; a direct lesson in grouping for charts and interfaces.
ambiguity: Scale contrast between the first bar and the stubs is also strong; the grouping reading rests on the bracket and the combined bar.

observations: Thick route lines in red, blue, black, green, yellow, orange, brown and violet cross a pale grey street map of London.
A reference box at the upper left pairs each railway name with a short sample of its line colour.
The title UNDERGROUND appears in large pale capitals on a black band across a green border.
effect: Giving each route a distinct saturated hue against the muted street map lets a reader trace one line through crossings and tell the routes apart.
teaching_value: An early transit map uses hue to separate overlapping routes and a key to name them; a wayfinding precedent for colour-coded navigation and interface legends.
ambiguity: Several hues (dark blue, black, brown) are close in value at small size; colour separation is clearer for the bright routes than the dark ones.

observations: The right-hand page shows four blocks of a bold sans-serif headed Gothic No. 2; each block opens with one large all-capital word such as COMMERCE or BENCH.
Below each capital word, mixed-case lines in the same face are set noticeably smaller.
The left-hand page is filled with small engraved stock cuts: ears, eyes, coffins, buildings and harness.
effect: Setting one large capital word over smaller lines in each block creates a clear typographic hierarchy, and the type page reads as bold against the busy engraved page.
teaching_value: A 1882 foundry specimen shows display type at several sizes with headline-and-subline pairs, a compact lesson in typographic hierarchy by size.
ambiguity: The spread pairing with the engraving page comes from the book's binding; only the type page is counted as the deliberate size hierarchy.

observations: One page repeats the same two-line unit, a mixed-case sentence and an all-capital line with numerals, eight times from 8 Point to 36 Point Bodoni Book.
Each unit is a little larger than the one above, and fewer words fit across the fixed measure as the size grows.
Thin orange vertical rules and an inch scale run across the whole block behind the type.
effect: Repeating one unit at steadily increasing sizes sets up a stepped beat down the page, so the reader compares sizes by rhythm rather than by reading.
teaching_value: A twentieth-century type specimen page shows a regular progressive series on a measured grid; a model for size ramps and type scales in layout and interface design.
ambiguity: This is a photograph of a printed specimen page; the CC BY licence is the photographer's. The progression is also a scale-contrast example.

observations: A large red triangle points from the upper left down to the right, its tip touching the edge of a white circle on a black field.
The sheet is split by a diagonal boundary between a white area at left and a black area at right.
Cyrillic words are set at angles: one runs downward at the upper left, another is rotated along the triangle's lower edge.
effect: Driving the red wedge and the rotated lettering along diagonals makes the composition read as forceful and in motion rather than static.
teaching_value: A 1919 lithographic poster builds its whole message from tilted geometric shapes and angled type, a foundational constructivist example of diagonal layout.
ambiguity: Colour contrast and value contrast are also strong; the political message is from source context, not established by this reading.

observations: A woman in a black dress and wide black hat fills the centre as one flat black shape with almost no interior detail.
Behind her, the stage, orchestra and a man in a top hat are drawn in yellow, grey and olive.
Hand-drawn lettering Divan Japonais runs across the top, and Ed Fournier directeur sits at lower left.
effect: Reducing the main figure to a large flat black mass against lighter colour makes her shape read instantly from a distance, which suits a street poster.
teaching_value: A colour lithograph poster from 1892-93 shows how a flat dark silhouette can anchor a poster and carry the composition with lettering around it.
ambiguity: The figure is a dark shape on a lighter scene rather than a backlit outline; the performer at the top is also cut off by the edge (tight cropping).

observations: The poster uses a small set of colours: orange and rust for the woman's cloak, a pale green curtain and portfolio, cream paper and dark blue outlines.
The same orange returns in the wall telephone, the floor and the lettering ESTAMPES & ENCADREMENTS D'ART.
A lettered band at the bottom reads N. LEMBREE AVENUE LOUISE 17 BRUXELLES in dark blue on cream.
effect: Repeating a few related colours across figure, room and lettering ties image and text into one calm, unified sheet.
teaching_value: An 1897 lithographic shop poster shows a restricted palette shared between illustration and lettering, a useful model for a small brand colour set.
ambiguity: Orange against pale green also gives some complementary contrast; the reading counts the repetition of a limited palette.

observations: The words SI and NO alternate in a line stepping from the upper left down to the lower right.
The first SI is small at the top-left corner; each later word is larger, ending in a SI with an accent that fills most of the right-hand height.
The ground is split horizontally into orange above and olive green below, with the letters in dark red and black.
effect: Letting the same short words grow from small to very large makes the last word dominate and gives the sequence a sense of rising emphasis.
teaching_value: A 1932 futurist book page makes typography itself the image, using escalating letter size to build emphasis; a direct reference for expressive display type.
ambiguity: The stepped descent also reads as a diagonal. This is a reproduction of a book page; any meaning beyond the printed words is not established here.

observations: A smiling woman in a red cloche hat and black coat is shown from the chest up, centred on a plain cream sheet with no background scene.
The red script word Igeha sits in the empty space at upper left and smaller black script Schokolade at upper right.
Large areas of blank cream remain above the hat and on both sides of the figure.
effect: Leaving the ground empty isolates the figure and gives the lettering clear room, so the product name and face read quickly.
teaching_value: A 1926 lithographed advertising poster shows how open space around one figure makes room for brand lettering, a pattern still used in posters and landing pages.
ambiguity: Visible product and brand names are historical and do not imply endorsement; the black coat also works as a silhouette.
